subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

options: The birth rate is higher than the death rate
The death rate is higher than the birth rate
questions.explain: Natural increase is birth rate minus death rate (excluding migration).

questions.q: The Demographic Transition Model (DTM) shows how:
options: Birth and death rates change as a country develops
questions.explain: The DTM models population change through stages of development.

questions.q: In the early stages of the DTM, both birth and death rates are:
questions.explain: Stage 1 has high, fluctuating birth and death rates and low population growth.

questions.q: An ageing population creates challenges such as:
options: More demand for healthcare and pensions with fewer workers
questions.explain: An ageing population raises the dependency ratio and pressures on services.

questions.q: A youthful population (many young people) can create pressure on:
questions.explain: A youthful population needs education and, later, employment opportunities.

options: The non-working population to the working population
questions.explain: It measures how many dependents (young and old) each worker supports.

questions.q: A country with a rapidly ageing population might respond by:
options: Raising the retirement age or encouraging migration of workers
questions.explain: Policies aim to balance the workforce and support dependents.

questions.q: As countries develop, death rates usually fall first because of:
options: Better healthcare, sanitation and food supply
questions.explain: Improved living conditions lower death rates before birth rates fall.

options: The general wellbeing of people, including health, education and environment
Only how much money someone has
questions.explain: Quality of life is broader than income, covering many aspects of wellbeing.

options: Differences in wealth and opportunity between groups or regions
questions.explain: Inequality can exist between regions, groups and individuals within a country.

questions.q: Improving access to education can raise quality of life by:
options: Increasing skills, employment and income over time
questions.explain: Education is a key driver of development and improved wellbeing.

questions.q: Access to clean water and sanitation mainly improves:
questions.explain: Clean water and sanitation cut waterborne disease and improve wellbeing.

questions.q: Regional inequality within a country might be reduced by:
options: Investing in poorer regions' jobs, transport and services
questions.explain: Targeted investment can narrow the gap between regions.
Immigration can offset ageing by adding workers, though it raises other issues.

questions.q: A government wanting to improve quality of life in a poor region should prioritise:
questions.explain: Basic services and infrastructure most improve wellbeing and opportunity.

questions.q: A population pyramid with a wide base indicates:
options: A high birth rate and a youthful population
questions.explain: A wide base shows many children — typical of a youthful, high-birth-rate population.
